messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Ravi is a 53-year-old South Asian American man who came to treatment after years of trying to keep his inner life tightly contained. He is married and works as a painter, spending most days on ladders, in half-finished rooms, with the sharp smell of thinner, turpentine, fresh paint, and dust around him. The event he returns to began before he immigrated to the United States, when he was a civilian living in a war zone. He describes being caught during shelling in a residential area, the kind of ordinary place where people had been trying to continue daily life despite the fighting. He remembers the sudden crack and blast of an explosion, the air changing all at once, the smell of smoke and burning rushing in, and his body dropping and folding in on itself as he tried to make himself small against the ground. What remains vivid is not just fear but the absolute lack of control: there had been nowhere safe to go, nothing useful to do, only the helpless knowledge that the next blast could come without warning. When he thinks of that day now, he can still feel his body taking the same position, bracing and tightening as if the danger is present again. Alongside that bodily memory comes a grief so intense that he sometimes stops speaking in session, as if words are too small for what was lost. At other times he says the whole thing feels unreal to him, “too extreme,” hard to believe it actually happened in his own life.

In the years afterward, Ravi did not talk much about the war. He threw himself into work and into the practical tasks of building a stable life. Keeping busy became his answer to almost everything. If he stayed occupied, took extra painting jobs, focused on trim lines and wall prep and cleanup, then he did not have to sit with questions that kept circling anyway: why did this happen to me, why was I there, why did my life become divided into before and after? He goes over these questions repeatedly, not arriving anywhere, but unable to leave them alone. He also began avoiding television coverage and online reports about bombings, wars, or civilians trapped in attacks. Even headlines are enough to make his chest tighten. He does not tell his wife much about this; he simply changes the channel, leaves the room, or says he is tired of the news.

His work exposes him to some of the very sensations that unsettle him most. On job sites, the smell of solvents or other chemical odors can hit him without warning and instantly place him back in that earlier scene of smoke and burning. Loud bangs are especially difficult. A dropped tool, a slammed metal door, construction noise from another unit, even a sudden pop outside can make him jolt so sharply that coworkers notice. He hates those moments. They leave him embarrassed and on edge, his body tense and prepared for danger long after everyone else has gone back to work. He scans constantly without fully meaning to—doorways, windows, sudden noises, movements in the hallway. He has come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that relaxing is a mistake. When plans change suddenly or he cannot control what is happening around him, he feels a rush of alarm that seems larger than the situation itself. What frightens him is that his body reacts first, before he can tell himself he is in America now, in a client’s living room, holding a paintbrush.

Over time these reactions have altered how he sees himself. Ravi had once understood himself as capable, steady, and able to provide through skill and discipline. Now he worries he is no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. Even when he completes jobs well, he does not feel restored by them. He says that nothing feels especially meaningful anymore; he keeps going because work must be done, bills must be paid, and his family depends on him, but inside there is a flatness that he cannot shake. His wife has noticed that he is always occupied and rarely at ease. He spends less time sitting with her in the evenings, especially if the television might carry footage of war or disaster, and she experiences him as physically present but hard to reach.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a recent incident at work when a sudden bang from a neighboring crew sent him into such an intense startle that he had to step down from the ladder and leave the room. The smell of paint thinner in the enclosed space stayed with him, and for a moment he felt not only the old bodily posture of bracing against the ground but the same overwhelming grief and disbelief, as if past and present had become confused. He was shaken by how quickly it happened and by the thought that he could not trust himself to stay steady. Coming to treatment, he says he wants some relief from being constantly on guard, but what he is most afraid of is that the war has permanently stripped life of meaning and left him living in a world that will never again feel safe.
